{{Short description|Inference rule that may be applied to only a particular segment of an expression}}In logic, a '''rule of replacement'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Copi |first1=Irving M. |last2=Cohen |first2=Carl |title=Introduction to Logic |publisher=Prentice Hall |year=2005}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=A Concise Introduction to Logic 4th edition |url=https://archive.org/details/studyguidetoacco00burc |url-access=registration |last=Hurley |first=Patrick  |year=1991 |publisher=Wadsworth Publishing |isbn=9780534145156 }}</ref><ref>Moore and Parker {{full|date=September 2019}}</ref> is a [[transformation rule]] that may be applied to only a particular segment of an [[well-formed formula|expression]]. A [[logical system]] may be constructed so that it uses either [[axiom]]s, [[rules of inference]], or both as transformation rules for [[Well-formed formula|logical expressions]] in the system. Whereas a rule of inference is always applied to a whole logical expression, a rule of replacement may be applied to only a particular segment. Within the context of a [[logical proof]], [[logically equivalent]] expressions may replace each other. Rules of replacement are used in [[propositional logic]] to manipulate [[proposition]]s.

Common rules of replacement include [[de Morgan's laws]], [[Commutative property|commutation]], association, distribution, [[double negation]],{{efn|not admitted in [[intuitionistic logic]]}} [[Transposition (logic)|transposition]], [[Material implication (rule of inference)|material implication]], [[logical equivalence]], [[Exportation (logic)|exportation]], and [[Tautology (rule of inference)|tautology]].

== Table: Rules of Replacement ==
The rules above can be summed up in the following table.<ref>Kenneth H. Rosen: ''Discrete Mathematics and its Applications'', Fifth Edition, p. 58.</ref> The "[[Tautology (logic)|Tautology]]" column shows how to interpret the notation of a given rule.
{| class="wikitable"
!Rules of inference
!Tautology
!Name
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
(p \vee q) \vee r\\
\therefore \overline{p \vee (q \vee r)} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>((p \vee q) \vee r) \rightarrow (p \vee (q \vee r))</math>
|[[Associative property#Propositional logic|Associative]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
p \wedge q\\
\therefore \overline{q \wedge p} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>(p \wedge q) \rightarrow (q \wedge p)</math>
|[[Commutative property#Propositional logic|Commutative]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
(p \wedge q) \rightarrow r\\
\therefore \overline{p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow r)} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>((p \wedge q) \rightarrow r) \rightarrow (p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow r))</math>
|[[Exportation (logic)|Exportation]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
p \rightarrow q\\
\therefore \overline{\neg q \rightarrow \neg p} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow (\neg q \rightarrow \neg p)</math>
|[[Transposition (logic)|Transposition or contraposition law]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
p \rightarrow q\\
\therefore \overline{\neg p \vee q} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>(p \rightarrow q) \rightarrow (\neg p \vee q)</math>
|[[Material implication (rule of inference)|Material implication]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
(p \vee q) \wedge r\\
\therefore \overline{(p \wedge r) \vee (q \wedge r)} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>((p \vee q) \wedge r) \rightarrow ((p \wedge r) \vee (q \wedge r))</math>
|[[Distributive property#Propositional logic|Distributive]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
p\\
q\\
\therefore \overline{p \wedge q} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>((p) \wedge (q))  \rightarrow (p \wedge q)</math>
|[[Logical conjunction|Conjunction]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
p\\
\therefore \overline{\neg \neg p} \\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>p \rightarrow (\neg \neg p)</math>
|[[Double negation|Double negation introduction]]
|-
|<math>\begin{align}
{\neg \neg p}\\
\therefore \overline p\\
\end{align}</math>
|<math>(\neg \neg p) \rightarrow p</math>
|[[Double negation elimination]]
|}
